strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: understanding and forecasting language-model learning curves through loss at individual token positions. The reciprocal position-loss model is compact and interpretable.

The descriptive results are promising. Across two model sizes trained for 400B tokens with checkpoints every 1B tokens, the paper reports positional fits with R² > 0.95 for over 99% of checkpoints. These observations support an empirical regularity within the studied setting.

The forecasting procedure is explicitly formulated, including continuity and derivative matching between training phases. Figure 1 reports lower forecast errors than the selected baselines across both model sizes and validation collections.

The position-weighting experiments extend the analysis beyond curve fitting, comparing three interventions across eight downstream benchmarks. Their similar average performance provides useful evidence about these particular training variants.
weaknesses: The central forecasting claim needs independent validation. Section 3.3 selects the separation point for its full-trajectory fit quality and derives the functional forms from the completed runs subsequently used for forecasting evaluation. Restricting coefficient fitting to early checkpoints does not eliminate dependence on those model-selection choices. The forecasting recipe should be fixed using development trajectories and evaluated on separate runs. This is a substantive soundness concern underlying the resubmission recommendation.

The baseline comparisons do not establish the benefit of modeling token positions. The proposed method explicitly incorporates the cosine learning-rate schedule, whereas the baselines use simpler functional forms. An essential comparison is fitting aggregate loss directly with the same piecewise logarithmic/cosine model and boundary conditions. Without this ablation, the improvement could primarily reflect schedule information. The power-law baseline is also labeled 'Exponential' without its exact equation being supplied.

The interpretation of uniform learning is too strong. Equation 16 follows algebraically from assuming that a0 and a1 become constant; it does not independently establish equal learning dynamics or the ineffectiveness of reweighting. Figure 4 offers supporting observations but averages over 32 neighboring positions. Three suppression strategies introduced after 100B tokens, without reported run variability or equivalence analysis, support only the narrower conclusion that these variants show no clear average advantage.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The appendix promised for fitted parameters is absent from the supplied manuscript, and no code or checkpoint-level loss data are linked. Nonlinear fitting procedures, initialization or constraints, training batch size, and weighting normalization are insufficiently specified. Batch size is needed to translate the 2,000 warmup steps into the token-based warmup variable. The separation point is also inconsistent: 40% of 400B is 160B, while Section 4.1 states 120B.

The evidence supports a narrower scope than the general temporal-scaling claims. Experiments use two relatively close model sizes, one training corpus, one training horizon, one learning-rate schedule, and 1,024-token evaluation sequences. Robustness to changes in these conditions is untested. The OOD designation also needs justification because the Pile includes Gutenberg/PG-19 material; held-out PG-19 books alone do not establish generalization to an unseen source domain.

The positioning and mathematical motivation require correction. Kaplan et al. already examine learning curves and dependence on training steps, so describing temporal behavior as previously untouched mischaracterizes prior work. The distinctive contribution should be the positional decomposition and proposed forecasting procedure. Additionally, Equation 5 is not a general probability ordering for consecutive realized tokens; an argument using expected conditional entropy would require explicit assumptions.
